newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK cigarette firms seen defending record.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK cigarette firms seen defending record.

text.p: Two British tobacco companies facing a new threat of legal action against the health effects of smoking cigarettes are set to maintain their longstanding robust defence of their record, industry experts said on Friday.
Forty cancer sufferers plan to sue Imperial Tobacco, about to be demerged from Hanson Plc, and American Brands Inc unit Gallaher, in a group action.

Their lawyers said the case would be based on the alleged failure of the firms -- which produce such brands as Benson and Hedges, Players, Embassy and Silk Cut -- to reduce the levels of tar in their cigarettes after doctors in the late 1950s began saying tar could lead to the onset of cancer.
Share analysts said the thrust of the case was not new, and was of a type the industry had successfully defended itself against in the past, but saw the lawyer's approach as new.
Despite being denied legal aid, the plaintiffs are to press on with their case because the lawyers representing them are prepared to work on a so-called "no-win, no-fee" basis.
"This is a step change in the litigation risk for firms," said Juliane Jessup, tobacco analyst at UBS in London.
She added that the availability of the approach, little used in British courts up to now, was set to be a boost for potential plaintiffs who have in the past faced prohibitive legal costs.
A flurry of new lawsuits would, inevitably, also mean higher defence costs for companies, she added. "If there are more cases it will be more expensive for the industry to defend."
However, analysts also doubted that the change of tack by plaintiffs would lead to anything other than a continued robust defence from the tobacco companies in Britain.
"It's fatal for these companies to settle out of court," said analyst Mark Duffy at SBC Warburg.

He added that if the cancer victims' cases come to court as a group action, as planned, historical experience from lawsuits in the United States and Britain suggested they would have a lower chance of success than taking action individually.
"If it is a group action, that seems a difficult way to go about it if you're a plaintiff," he said.
In particular, he pointed out, tobacco companies' lawyers had often managed to expose variances in plaintiffs' injuries and circumstances that undermined the "commonality" of claims.
Along with other analysts, Duffy nevertheless saw no reason for cigarette companies to be complacent and simply rest on their past record in beating back such lawsuits.

Several analysts said that investors should be aware of the potential costs that could come from cases known as "failure to warn" in which plaintiffs claim that tobacco firms' knew of health risks in the past but did not provide warnings.

Experience to date suggests that such cases need more than injured parties and anecdotal evidence to make them stick, and that evidence in the form of so-called "smoking gun" testimony from disgruntled employees, or in documents, may be key.

The main conclusions share analysts draw from the latest UK move, therefore, are that the use of the British legal system is catching up, perhaps equal to where the U.S. was 20 years ago, and that British firms should be steeled for more cases.
"This has to be factored into the Imperial Tobacco valuation," SBC's Duffy said, refering to the market's likely approach to the Hanson unit, due to start trading next Tuesday.
"Maybe the share's yield premium should be 50 percent rather than the 40 percent (initially considered right)," he added.
This would still be below the extra risk factor, compared to the wider share market, seen in companies heavily-exposed to the U.S. legal scene, he added.
Britain's B.A.T Industries Plc, for example, is heavily involved in the U.S. cigarette market and its shares yield a premium of about 70 percent over the market.
